result.claim: Why might global trade imbalances worsen, and can the U.S. keep absorbing the world's surplus savings?
result.reason: Global surpluses must be matched by deficits somewhere, so the question is who absorbs them and for how long.

result.excerpt: If China, the euro area, and Japan all have significant surpluses, someone big needs to have a significant deficit for global trade to add up.
result.claim: Global current accounts must sum to zero, so large surpluses in Europe and Asia require a large deficit elsewhere, chiefly the U.S.
result.reason: World surpluses and deficits must net to zero.

result.excerpt: As a result, trade imbalances run mostly along an east-west axis these days.
result.claim: With low oil prices and U.S. shale, the commodity (north-south) component of imbalances has shrunk, leaving them mostly east-west.
result.reason: When commodity prices fall, commodity exporters' surpluses shrink and their share of imbalances recedes.

result.excerpt: the gap between European fiscal policy and U.S. fiscal policy is a major cause of the transatlantic imbalances
result.claim: Divergent fiscal stances, tight in Europe and loose in the U.S., drive the transatlantic imbalance.
result.reason: A country's fiscal deficit lowers national saving relative to investment and widens its external deficit.

result.excerpt: he doesn't attribute trade outcomes to fiscal policy choices
result.claim: The Trump administration does not see trade outcomes as the product of fiscal policy choices.
result.reason: Trade balances reflect macroeconomic saving and investment choices, not just trade policy.

result.excerpt: With demand in short supply globally, negative interest rates in Europe and Japan, and real interest rates globally at very low levels, I would put more emphasis on the European side
result.claim: Given weak global demand and very low rates, the adjustment should come from European fiscal expansion, not U.S. tightening.
result.reason: When demand is scarce and rates are near zero, surplus countries should expand rather than deficit countries contract.

result.excerpt: But still Germany ran a (gulp) 2.7 pp of GDP fiscal surplus in the first half of the year.
result.claim: Northern European countries remain fiscally tight: Germany runs a 2.7% of GDP surplus, Sweden refuses to loosen, and Switzerland prefers intervention; EU debt rules push others toward surpluses.
result.reason: Persistent fiscal surpluses in surplus economies sustain their external surpluses.

result.excerpt: Maybe European fiscal policy is about to change—Mario Draghi certainly thinks it should.
result.claim: European fiscal policy might shift, given Draghi's advocacy and Germany's evolving debate, which would ease the transatlantic imbalance.
result.reason: Policy debates can shift quickly in recessions, so current fiscal stances may not persist.

result.excerpt: They both run tight fiscal policies when they don't need to and also give their manufacturing heavy economies a boost with weak currencies
result.claim: Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Thailand are the easy cases in Asia: tight fiscal policy plus currency intervention, direct or indirect, sustain their surpluses.
result.reason: Undervalued currencies held down by intervention, combined with fiscal restraint, generate external surpluses.

result.excerpt: Their external surpluses don't fit easily into a global narrative where imbalances stem primarily from differences in national fiscal policy.
result.claim: Japan and China run loose fiscal policies yet still have surpluses, so fiscal differences alone cannot explain Asia's imbalances.
result.reason: A cause that explains some cases must be tested against the cases it does not fit.

result.excerpt: Contrary to most forecasts, China is once again running a substantial current account surplus.
result.claim: Forecasts expected China's surplus to fade, yet it is back near $200-250 billion.
result.reason: An outcome contradicting consensus forecasts signals a missing factor in the standard model.

result.excerpt: more accurate measures of the tourism deficit would put the surplus at around $250 billion
result.claim: China's measured surplus of under $200 billion understates the true figure; correcting the overstated tourism deficit gives about $250 billion.
result.reason: Correct known measurement errors in official balance of payments components before drawing conclusions.

result.excerpt: Countries with 12 percent of GDP fiscal deficits usually run large external deficits.
result.claim: Countries with fiscal deficits of around 12% of GDP normally run large external deficits.
result.reason: Large fiscal deficits typically spill over into external deficits.

result.excerpt: that surplus has been sustained even with a 12 percent of GDP "augmented" fiscal deficit
result.claim: Using the IMF's augmented deficit of 12% of GDP, which includes local government vehicle borrowing, rather than the 3-5% headline figures, is the right measure of China's fiscal stance.
result.reason: Fiscal stance should include quasi-fiscal borrowing by off-budget public entities.

result.excerpt: namely that China saves way too much. In fact, China still saves about two times as much as a typical large economy
result.claim: China's surplus despite huge fiscal deficits shows that it saves excessively, about twice a typical large economy.
result.reason: A surplus that persists despite fiscal dissaving implies very high private saving.

result.excerpt: the aggregated savings rate of East Asia is as high as it has ever been—it remains close to 40 percent of the region's GDP.
result.claim: East Asia saves close to 40% of GDP; China's rate fell from 51% to 44%, but its regional weight rose from 49% to 72%; China now saves about $6 trillion a year versus $2 trillion in 2007.
result.reason: Composition shifts toward a high-saving economy can keep aggregate saving high even as its own rate falls.

result.excerpt: The only thing preventing that high savings rate from turning into a much larger current account surplus is China's large augmented fiscal deficit and the associated high level of public investment.
result.claim: China's big augmented fiscal deficit and public investment are all that keep its high saving from producing a far larger surplus.
result.reason: The current account equals saving minus investment, so high saving is offset only by high investment or dissaving.

result.excerpt: So long as China's adjustment is based on a set of fiscal (and credit) policies that are generally viewed as unsustainable
result.claim: China's adjustment rests on unsustainable fiscal and credit expansion, so its durability is doubtful.
result.reason: An adjustment financed by unsustainable borrowing will reverse when that borrowing stops.

result.claim: The fiscal and credit policies currently absorbing China's savings cannot continue, and nothing else will reduce household saving unless policy changes.
result.reason: Structural saving is persistent unless income distribution or social insurance changes.

result.excerpt: China's import growth has collapsed—imports are falling in nominal terms, and at best flat in real terms.
result.claim: China's 2019 stimulus was modest, with a flat credit impulse after a negative one in 2018, and imports are falling, which has pushed the surplus back up.
result.reason: Withdrawing stimulus in a high-saving economy cuts imports and enlarges its surplus.

result.excerpt: the fall off in new investment in manufacturing associated with the trade war has contributed (ironically) to the rise in China's surplus
result.claim: The trade war, by depressing Chinese manufacturing investment, ironically raised China's surplus.
result.reason: Lower domestic investment, with saving unchanged, raises the current account surplus.

result.excerpt: A more sustainable adjustment requires policies that raise household income and reduce savings—basically more progressive tax policies and a much bigger system of social insurance
result.claim: China should raise household income and cut saving through progressive taxes and a larger, non-regressively funded social insurance system.
result.reason: Lasting cuts in excess saving require shifting income to households and reducing precautionary saving.

result.excerpt: The current "flow" deficit in the United States external accounts isn't obviously unsustainable.
result.claim: The U.S. current account deficit stays under 3% of GDP, helped by the oil boom and offshore profits, and debt is stable because interest rates are below nominal growth.
result.reason: Debt ratios stay stable when the interest rate on debt is below nominal growth.

result.excerpt: At 45 percent of U.S. GDP, it is actually quite large relative to the United States' limited export base.
result.claim: U.S. net external debt is about 45% of GDP, triple its level of twenty years ago, against a non-commodity export base of only about 8% of GDP.
result.reason: External debt sustainability is judged relative to the export base that must service it.

result.excerpt: Especially if you assume that the United States won't be a long-run exporter of energy
result.claim: The U.S. will not be a long-run net energy exporter, because of high domestic demand and a slow transition to low carbon.
result.reason: Only durable export sources should count toward a country's capacity to service external debt.

result.excerpt: Trump or no Trump. that at some point will limit its ability to take the other side of the world's saving surpluses.
result.claim: With Asian, especially Chinese, excess saving likely to resurface and Europe fiscally tight, imbalances could worsen, while rising U.S. external debt will eventually limit America's ability to absorb them.
result.reason: A deficit country's capacity to absorb others' surpluses is bounded by its accumulated external debt.

result.excerpt: they want the euro area to continue to tighten but only by a bit, while the US would tighten by a lot
result.claim: The IMF plans to reduce imbalances mainly through U.S. fiscal tightening alongside slight euro area tightening, with fiscal balance as the long-run norm.
result.reason: Adjustment that falls on deficit countries in a demand-short world shrinks imbalances by depressing demand.
